title: Circuit fault clinic
subtitle: Which materials complete the loop?
objective: Use a checked low-voltage circuit to compare electrical conductors and insulators.

sow.exactOutcome: Investigate thermal and electrical conductors and insulators.
sow.alignment: Directly develops the stated science outcome. Original secondary-age exemplar activities; diagnostic-led support and stretch follow the SoW. No claim of qualification approval.

priorLearning: Recognise a cell, a lamp and connecting wires.
Know that materials have properties useful for different jobs.
Thermal conductivity and electrical conductivity are different properties; do not treat the thermal test as an electrical result.
success: Describe a complete conducting loop through the cell, lamp and sample.
Use a known-conductor check before interpreting an unlit lamp.
Choose conductor and insulation materials for a lead, using test evidence.

vocabulary.meaning: A material through which electric charge can move readily.
A material through which electric charge moves much less readily.
The rate of flow of electric charge.
A connected loop through which a current can flow.
A known test used to check that the method or equipment works.

equipment: Paper route: common evidence page, selected pupil response route and pencils.
Optional practical per pair: one 1.5 V AA cell in a school holder, matching 1.5 V lamp and holder, switch, four insulated crocodile-clip leads.
Safe prepared dry samples: bare copper strip, aluminium foil strip with folded edges, dry card, rigid plastic strip; optional prepared coated-metal sample.
preparation: Teacher checks complete kit, cell condition, matching lamp rating and all leads before the lesson. Use the school-approved low-voltage kit and local procedure.
Prepare a known copper test strip with good contact surfaces. Check it immediately before and after the sample sequence.
Prepare samples and pupil copies in advance. Use the full paper route if any practical kit is unavailable. Do not substitute loose LEDs without the correct circuit.
safety: Use only the single 1.5 V cell and matching school lamp circuit described; never use mains sockets, plugs or electrical appliances.
Keep the lamp in series. Never join cell terminals directly with wire or a metal sample; this can heat the cell and leads.
Switch off before changing samples. If any component becomes warm, disconnect safely and tell the teacher.
Use dry prepared solid samples only. Do not test bodies, liquids or unknown objects; do not dismantle cables or scrape coatings.
Keep components out of mouths; teacher manages damaged cells and sharp or broken materials.
practicalAlternative: The complete paper fault-clinic uses supplied constructed observations and circuit diagrams. It assesses interpretation and design without handling electrical equipment.

misconceptions.claim: An unlit lamp proves the sample is an insulator.
misconceptions.correction: A faulty circuit or poor contact can also prevent light. Check a known conductor before and after the test.
misconceptions.check: Present the failed copper-control card; ask whether the sample can be classified.

misconceptions.claim: The lamp uses up the current.
misconceptions.correction: In this steady series loop the current is the same at each point. Energy is transferred by the lamp; charge is not used up.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether a second wire is needed to complete the loop.

misconceptions.correction: Many common dry non-metals are poor conductors, but graphite is a conducting non-metal.
misconceptions.check: Use the supplied stretch meter evidence; never increase voltage to make a class sample conduct.

misconceptions.claim: A material is safe to touch at any voltage if the little lamp does not light.
misconceptions.correction: This low-voltage result is not a general safety test. A small or undetected current can still exist; conditions and voltage matter.
misconceptions.check: Ask whether school test results permit touching household wires. They do not.

access.supported: Use page 2: trace the loop, classify three provided observations and complete one cable sentence. Read or scribe as required.
access.standard: Use page 3: interpret the whole result table, diagnose a failed control and justify both cable layers.
access.stretch: Use the Stretch route: evaluate lamp sensitivity and a graphite counterexample, then qualify the electrical-property claim. Same objective, more demanding evidence.
access.regulation: Pairs may choose checker, recorder or observer roles. Provide a seated paper route and quiet independent response. Never require touching or handling for participation; no timed wiring contest.

sources.title: Institute of Physics: Conductors and insulators
sources.note: Checked 9 September 2026. Conductivity is not an absolute two-category boundary; low-voltage lamp results must not imply human safety.

sources.title: Institute of Physics: Electric circuits and fields guidance notes
sources.note: Checked 9 September 2026. Teacher equipment checks, simple series-circuit troubleshooting and distinction between current and transferred energy. Use modern school kit guidance, not historical battery advice.

sources.title: National Grid: Conductors and insulators education resource
sources.note: Checked 9 September 2026. Supports a low-voltage material-gap test and graphite as a conducting non-metal. This original lesson excludes hazardous or unsuitable listed materials.

slides.title: You are the circuit fault team
body: A lamp is dark. Is the sample the problem?
Your job: check the evidence before classifying it.
Use a paper investigation or supervised low-voltage kit.
slides.notes: Explain the repair-clinic brief. Success is a defensible diagnosis, not fastest construction. Establish that no real appliances, mains equipment, bodies or liquids are tested.

slides.title: Find the missing idea
body: R1. Name a cell, lamp and wire.
R2. Does one wire from a cell to a lamp make a complete loop?
R3. Are thermal and electrical conductivity the same test?
slides.notes: R1 point to components in the next diagram if names are unfamiliar. R2 no: the loop must connect both cell terminals through the lamp. R3 no: thermal concerns energy transfer due to temperature difference; electrical concerns current. This lesson investigates electrical behaviour.

slides.title: Trace the whole loop
body: The sample bridges a gap in the circuit.
The lamp stays in the loop.
A good connection is needed at every join.
slides.notes: 8 minutes shared across three I do slides. Trace from one cell terminal, through wire, sample, lamp and closed switch to the other terminal. This is one cell, not a mains supply. The diagram has a switch shown closed. Teacher demonstrates known copper first; with valid kit it lights. Current is not used up by the lamp; electrical energy is transferred there.

visual.title: A complete test loop
visual.description: A simple series test circuit with one 1.5 V cell, a matching lamp, closed switch and sample bridging the gap. The lamp remains in the loop so the sample never directly joins the cell terminals.

elements.text: Every part must make a conducting connection

slides.title: One lead needs two properties
body: Copper provides a conducting path.
Plastic insulates the outside.
Both material choices serve a different purpose.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Think aloud: I need charge to move along the inside, so copper is useful. I want to reduce unwanted contact with that conducting path, so suitable insulation covers it. The enlarged cutaway is explanatory only. A classroom result does not certify insulation for real wiring.

visual.title: Different jobs in one cable
visual.description: Simplified cutaway of a low-voltage lead: copper inner conductor provides a current path; plastic outer insulation reduces unwanted contact. This is a diagram, not an instruction to strip a cable.

elements.text: Choose a material for its job

Cutaway model: sizes are enlarged.
Do not cut or open real electrical cables.

slides.title: Do not trust a single dark lamp
body: Check copper before the sample.
Check the sample contact, then observe.
Check copper again afterwards.
slides.notes: Shared I do time. Show the contact diagram. If clips touch paint, the test has not reached the metal underneath. Do not ask pupils to scrape it. If either copper check fails, stop: repair the circuit before classifying anything. Lamp brightness is an indicator with a detection limit, not proof of exactly zero current.

visual.title: A no-glow result needs a check
visual.description: Two views of a coated metal sample. Clips touching the coating have no reliable connection to the metal core; clips touching prepared exposed ends can make contact. Only the teacher uses a ready-prepared safe sample.

elements.text: Are the clips touching the material we mean?

Clips touch coating.
Metal core is not connected.
Result: uncertain for the metal.

Clips touch exposed metal.
Check with a known conductor.
Then interpret the lamp.
Use prepared samples only. No scraping or cutting.

slides.title: Fault clinic: sort the case cards
body: Use the five cases on page 1.
Sort: conductor evidence / insulator evidence / uncertain.
Give the exact clue that supports your decision.
slides.notes: 8 minutes shared across the We do slides. Pair roles: evidence reader and diagnostic checker; one person can work silently. Cases A copper lit, B dry plastic dark with controls pass, C foil dark but control fails, D painted metal dark with clips on paint, E bare aluminium lights. Expected categories: A/E conductor; B poor conductor or insulator in this tested circuit; C/D uncertain.

slides.title: Repair the reasoning, not the sample
body: C: foil dark; copper control also dark.
D: coated metal dark; clips touch the coating.
What should we do before making a claim?
slides.notes: Shared We do time. C: disconnect and teacher checks cell, lamp, leads and switch, then repeat known conductor and sample. D: use a safe prepared sample with proper contact to the intended material, or mark uncertain. Do not scrape, cut, add cells or bypass the lamp. A fault clinic values the answer not enough evidence.
slides.reveal: C: check the circuit. D: check which material the clips actually touch.

slides.title: Build the class evidence table
body: Constructed observations from a checked 1.5 V circuit.
Known copper lights before and after this sequence.
Use “in this test” when classifying dark results.
slides.notes: Shared We do time. All samples dry, contacts valid, same kit; these are constructed observations. Ask which two materials provide conductor evidence and which two support poor-conductor classification. The lamp does not rank copper versus aluminium quantitatively.

table.caption: Constructed sample observations; copper controls passed before and after.

slides.title: The control fails. What now?
body: A plastic sample gives no glow. The copper control also gives no glow.
slides.notes: Collect an independent choice. If A or C selected, point to the failed known conductor. If D selected, remind pupils never to raise voltage or bypass checks. Repair logic before You do.

options.feedback: No. The copper control also failed, so the circuit may be faulty.

options.text: Check the circuit, then repeat the tests.
options.feedback: Yes. A passing control is needed before interpreting the sample result.
No. A faulty lamp, cell, lead or contact is a more relevant explanation to check.

options.text: Add many more cells to force a result.
options.feedback: No. Keep to the approved low-voltage kit and ask the teacher to check it.

slides.title: Make your diagnostic report
body: Choose one response route with page 1 beside it.
Interpret the evidence, then design a two-layer lead.
State one result that must remain uncertain.
slides.notes: 10 minutes shared over three You do slides. Optional pairs may test four prepared materials within this interval: teacher supplies checked loop, then pupils change one sample with switch off, observe and record. Paper route is complete without the practical. Actual observations may differ: record them honestly and diagnose, do not overwrite them with the supplied examples.

slides.title: If using the optional kit
body: Copper check → sample → record → copper check.
Switch off for changes; keep the lamp in series.
Unexpected result? Mark uncertain and ask the teacher.
slides.notes: Shared You do time. A 10-minute test is possible only with preassembled checked kit and prepared samples. Any delay: use the provided observation cards immediately. Do not add curriculum content or compromise the review to chase a working bulb.

slides.title: Use a scientific conclusion
body: “The lamp lit, which supports …”
“No glow with valid controls supports … in this test.”
“The control failed, so I cannot yet …”
slides.notes: Shared You do time. Ask for evidence and reason. Supported pupils may dictate. Stretch note: graphite with a very small meter-detected current may fail to visibly light this lamp; zero visible light is not the same as zero current. No meter practical required.

slides.title: Compare diagnoses
body: Which uncertain case changed your mind?
Explain why a good scientist may pause a conclusion.
Match conductor and insulation to their jobs.
slides.notes: 4 minutes shared across two Review slides. Expected response: a failed control means the setup cannot yet diagnose the sample. Copper inside and plastic outside meet different functions. Accept aluminium inside if evidence linked; avoid claims about suitability for all real cable manufacturing.

slides.title: Use our voice to improve the test
body: Choose the class’s most useful next improvement.
Options: clearer contacts, repeated checks, clearer recording.
Explain how your choice improves the evidence.
slides.notes: Light Lundy loop: pupils can point, write or speak. Teacher notes the chosen improvement and explains how the next investigation will use it. Do not make a popularity vote determine a scientific fact.

slides.title: Exit diagnosis
body: E1. Why must the circuit be a complete loop?
E2. Why check copper before and after a sample?
E3. Choose inside and outside materials for a lead.
slides.notes: E1 current needs a connected conducting path through this loop. E2 confirms kit works throughout; failed checks invalidate the classification. E3 copper/aluminium inside, appropriate plastic insulation outside, with jobs explained. Ask one transfer question next lesson if response is only a material list.

pupilPages.title: 1 • Shared evidence: circuit fault clinic
pupilPages.intro: All observations on this page are constructed sample observations from a 1.5 V cell and matching lamp. No real appliance is tested.

cards.title: Case A • Copper
cards.text: Bare copper lights the lamp. Copper control works before and after. Clips have sound contact.

cards.title: Case B • Dry plastic
cards.text: No visible glow. Copper control lights before and after. Clips touch the dry plastic correctly.

cards.title: Case C • Foil
cards.text: No visible glow. The copper control also gives no glow after the test.

cards.title: Case D • Coated metal
cards.text: No visible glow. Copper controls work, but both clips touch paint rather than the metal core.

cards.title: Case E • Aluminium
cards.text: Bare aluminium lights the lamp. Copper controls work before and after; contact is sound.

blocks.prompt: W1. Sort A–E into conductor evidence, insulator evidence in this test, or uncertain. Explain two decisions.
W2. For C and D, what should the teacher check before a material claim?

blocks.text: Additional constructed observations for the response routes: dry card has no visible glow with valid contacts and passing copper checks. Copper and bare aluminium light; rigid dry plastic does not visibly light. These observations do not measure exact conductivity.

pupilPages.title: 2 • Supported route: build a sound claim
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. Point, draw or dictate if useful. Use the same scientific goal.

blocks.prompt: S1. List or draw the cell, lamp and sample in one connected loop. Does a gap in a wire help the lamp light?
S2. Complete the three rows using the case evidence.
S3. Complete: Case C is uncertain because the ____ also failed. The teacher should check the ____ before testing again.
S4. Choose copper or plastic for each job. Inside path: ____ because ____ . Outer cover: ____ because ____ .
S5. Does no visible glow prove exactly zero current, or only that this lamp did not visibly light? Explain or point.

pupilPages.title: 3 • Standard route: a diagnostic report
pupilPages.intro: Use all cases on page 1. A sound report separates valid evidence from an uncertain result.

blocks.prompt: N1. Complete the observation and classification table. Refer to controls or contact where relevant.
N2. Write a safe three-step checking sequence before classifying an unlit result.

pupilPages.title: 3 continued • Standard route: the material decision
pupilPages.intro: Continue the same route. Use the common evidence page.

blocks.prompt: N3. Draw a cable cross-section. Label a suitable inner conductor and outer insulator. Explain both material choices.
N4. Why does a dark lamp not prove a material is safe at mains voltage?
N5. Can these observations tell you whether copper conducts exactly twice as well as aluminium? Explain.

pupilPages.title: 4 • Stretch route: when the indicator misses a current
pupilPages.intro: Use page 1. This is supplied evidence, not an instruction to change the classroom circuit.

blocks.text: Constructed evidence from a separate, teacher-controlled measuring circuit: a sensitive current meter detects a small current through graphite. The same lamp gives no visible glow. Checks before and after work. Graphite is a form of carbon and is not a metal.

blocks.prompt: T1. Evaluate: “Only metals can conduct electricity.” Use the graphite evidence.
T2. Explain why a lamp can miss a conducting sample. What does no visible glow actually tell you?

pupilPages.title: 4 continued • Stretch route: a stronger test
pupilPages.intro: Continue the same route. Use the common evidence page.

blocks.prompt: T3. Design a fair comparison of two prepared solid samples with the approved lamp circuit. Include the control checks, contact check and a limitation of this method.
T4. Use cases C and D to explain two different reasons why an unlit lamp may lead to an uncertain classification.
T5. Justify an inner conducting path and an insulating outer layer for a low-voltage lead. Include one limit of what our test can certify.

pupilPages.title: 5 • Exit and investigation record
pupilPages.intro: Record your own reasoning. If you performed a practical, label observations as your results; otherwise write paper evidence route.

blocks.prompt: E1. Why is a connected conducting loop needed in our lamp circuit?
E2. What do the known-copper checks tell you?
E3. Name a useful inside and outside material for a lead and explain their jobs.
E4. What would you improve next time to make a diagnosis more trustworthy?
Reflection. A claim I changed or qualified was …

answers.label: R1–R3
answers.answer: R1 cell provides the electrical supply, lamp is the light-emitting component, wires make connections. R2 no: there must be a complete loop through both cell terminals and the lamp. R3 no: thermal and electrical conductivity are distinct properties, investigated differently.

answers.label: W1 / cases A–E
answers.answer: A and E give conductor evidence: bare copper/aluminium light the lamp with controls and contacts valid. B supports classification as a poor conductor/insulator under this low-voltage test: dry plastic gives no visible glow with passing controls. C is uncertain because the known-conductor control fails. D is uncertain for the metal core because clips touch coating; the test concerns the contacted surface.

answers.label: W2
answers.answer: C: teacher disconnects, checks cell, lamp, leads and switch, restores passing copper check, then repeats the sample and control. D: teacher supplies a safe prepared sample with sound contact to exposed intended material, or records uncertain. Do not scrape/cut samples, add cells or bypass the lamp.

answers.label: We do table
answers.answer: Copper and bare aluminium provide conductor evidence; dry card and rigid plastic are poor conductors/insulators in this tested setup. No visible glow does not demonstrate zero current or electrical safety at other voltages. These observations are not a quantitative ranking of metals.

answers.label: Hinge A–D
answers.answer: A wrong: the failed copper check means the plastic cannot yet be blamed. B correct: check circuit and repeat with passing controls. C wrong: investigate equipment/contact rather than claiming copper became an insulator. D wrong: do not add cells; keep the stated safe kit and refer to teacher.

answers.label: S1–S2
answers.answer: S1 cell, lamp and sample joined in a loop through both cell terminals; an air gap interrupts it and prevents a visible lamp current in this kit. S2 A lights/conductor; B no glow/insulator evidence in this test; C no glow/uncertain because control failed.

answers.label: S3–S5
answers.answer: S3 copper control; circuit. S4 copper inner path because charge can move readily; plastic outer cover because it resists charge movement and reduces unwanted contact. S5 only that this lamp did not visibly light; very small current may be below the lamp indication threshold.

answers.label: N1
answers.answer: Copper A: lit, conductor, valid controls. Plastic B: no visible glow, insulator evidence in this test, valid controls and contacts. Foil C: no visible glow, uncertain, failed control. Coated metal D: no glow, uncertain for metal, clips touch paint. Aluminium E: lit, conductor, valid controls.

answers.label: N2–N3
answers.answer: N2 with switch off use known copper and then switch on to confirm kit works; switch off, connect the prepared dry sample with sound contact and observe; switch off and restore copper, then verify the control still works. Accept equivalent sequence including no bypass of lamp. N3 diagram labels conducting inner copper/aluminium and insulating outer plastic; explain current path and reduced unwanted contact. No real cable dismantling.

answers.label: N4–N5
answers.answer: N4 low-voltage no-glow results do not establish no current under all conditions. Higher voltages and different conditions can be hazardous; never test mains equipment or bodies. N5 no: visible lamp observations are qualitative, not a measured conductivity ratio. Quantitative comparison needs suitable measurements and controlled sample dimensions and conditions.

answers.label: T1–T2
answers.answer: T1 reject only metals: graphite is a non-metal and the meter detects a current. T2 the small current may be below that needed for visible lamp glow. A dark lamp reports no visible light in this circuit, not mathematically zero current. Do not increase class voltage to seek a response.

answers.label: T3–T4
answers.answer: T3 same cell, lamp, leads, sample length/contact spacing and safe contact quality; change sample, check known copper before and after, switch off for changes, record observations and repeat. Limitation: lamp threshold and sample geometry mean qualitative evidence, not exact intrinsic conductivity. T4 C has failed equipment/control validity; D lacks valid contact with the intended metal core.

answers.label: T5
answers.answer: Conducting inner copper or aluminium enables the current path; insulating outer material helps isolate it. These class observations cannot certify a product for mains wiring, durability or all voltages, nor prove zero leakage current.

answers.label: E1–E4 / optional record
answers.answer: E1 a connected conducting path is needed around this circuit for a lamp current. E2 establishes the kit worked immediately before and after sample testing; failures require rechecking. E3 copper/aluminium conducting interior; suitable plastic insulating exterior, with functions. E4 relevant improvements: check contacts, repeat with controls, separate observation and inference. Optional actual-test record has no fixed observations: assess truthful recording and sound inference, including uncertain when controls fail. Reflection accepts any evidence-linked revision.

answers.label: Assessment / re-teach
answers.answer: Secure objective: can trace complete loop, interprets a dark result only after passing controls and valid contacts, and justifies conductor/insulator functions. A material sort without controls is incomplete. Re-teach with Case C beside A: same known copper, different lamp response. Ask what changed about the evidence before retesting conceptual understanding.

teacherNotes: 40-minute sequence: 2 opening + 3 retrieval + 8 I do + 8 We do + 3 hinge + 10 You do + 4 review + 2 exit. Zero-minute slides share the stage allocation.
The lesson is complete on paper. Optional kit work requires prepared checked apparatus and teacher supervision, and should not displace independent reasoning or exit evidence.
Keep thermal and electrical meanings separate. Some materials are good conductors of both, but this does not make the two processes identical.
Circuit drawing is a simplified representation with exaggerated component sizes; charge carriers and fields are not visible. The cable is a model cutaway, never a prompt to strip wire.

Treat classifications as useful relative descriptions under given conditions. No lamp glow is evidence of poor conduction only once contacts and known-conductor checks pass. No result here certifies electrical safety.
